newsitem.title: UK: ATHLETICS-BRITISH ATHLETICS PLUNGES DEEP INTO CRISIS.
newsitem.headline: ATHLETICS-BRITISH ATHLETICS PLUNGES DEEP INTO CRISIS.

text.p: British athletics, the envy of the world four years ago, has plunged deep into crisis with the unexpected resignation of executive chairman Peter Radford.
Radford, who only last week spoke confidently of the sport's bright future, has become the fourth chief executive in 15 years to quit after a nightmare two years at the helm.
"He's taken it to the edge of the abyss, then opened the parachute and jumped," said former British Athletic Federation (BAF) spokesman Tony Ward.
Where did it all go wrong?
At the 1993 Stuttgart world championships, Linford Christie crushed the leading Americans for the second in a row over 100 metres.
His friend and training partner Colin Jackson did the same in the high hurdles with a world record and there was yet another world record for Sally Gunnell in the women's 400 metres hurdles.
In the following year Radford, a former world record holder over 200 metres, exchanged the academic life for the high profile job of British athletics chief.
His problems started almost from the minute he took his post at the BAF's headquarters in Birmingham.
Promotions officer Andy Norman was dismissed over allegations surrounding the suicide of athletics writer Cliff Temple.

Director of coaching Frank Dick resigned in a row over funding and shot putter Paul Edwards and middle-distance runner Diane Modahl were flown home early from the Victoria Commonwealth Games after positive drugs tests were revealed.

In 1995, Christie and Jackson had a protracted and well-publicised row with the BAF over appearance money. Neither was among the medals at last year's Atlanta Olympics while Gunnell was stretchered from the track in the semifinals.
Although final figures are not available, the BAF is estimated to have lost 750,000 pounds sterling ($120,000) over the past two seasons through falling attendances and television revenue.
In addition Modahl, who drug ban was over-turned last March, is suing the BAF and plans to subpoena Radford.

"Diane and I are celebrating because it's great news," said Modahl's husband and coach Vicente on hearing the news of Radford's resignation. "Peter Radford was an absolute disaster for British athletics."
The BAF management board met last Thursday and later issued a bland statement saying it had agreed on a departure date for Radford.
But as yet no heir-apparent is on the horizon.
Brendan Foster, the 1976 Olympic 10,000 metres bronze medallist, who now runs a sports promotion company publicly ruled himself out of the running.
"I wouldn't wish the job on my worst enemy," Foster said. "No sensible person would be interested in the job of executive chairman.
"British athletics is like a cannibal, it eats its young."
Director of coaching Malcolm Arnold said it was essential to a have chief executive who understood the sport but conceded the job might be impossible to perform satisfactorily.
"If you don't understand the politics of the sport, you can just drop down into a big hole," he said. "I think it's a flawed model but I don't know what the model is."
The BAF is pinning its hopes for future development on its request for up to five million pounds sterling ($8,000,000) of national lottery money.
If the request is approved by the Sports Council, Arnold plans to increase the number of full-time coaches from 10 to 44 as part of a four-year plan culminating in the 2000 Sydney Olympics.
In the meantime, he has launched a robust defence of the BAF's record.
Arnold said although no British athlete had won a title in Atlanta, the men's team had finished fourth, the women's 11th and the combined position was sixth out of 197 nations.
"The thing that upset me most was that we didn't have an Olympic champion," he said.
He also attacked the public perception of athletics in Britain.
"Tim Henman goes out in the third round of the Australian Open and he's lionised," Arnold said.

"It's not really an athletics country if you lionise a tennis player who doesn't get to the semifinals of the Australian Open and a football team that gets knocked out in the semifinals of the European Cup."
